reponse:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A discrete quality distribution head trained from pairwise preferences
PROPOSAL: We replace the scalar value head of a discriminative reward model with a head that outputs a categorical distribution over five quality levels, and we train it on pairwise data from Skywork-Reward-Preference and HelpSteer2 with a Bradley-Terry likelihood applied to the expected level of each response, plus an entropy term that keeps the distribution from collapsing. The expected level is the score, the spread of the distribution is the confidence, and the head needs one forward pass per response, so Best-of-N scoring needs no pairwise formatting. We fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-instruct and Gemma-2-9B-it backbones and evaluate ranking accuracy on RewardBench and RM-Bench, and Best-of-N gains on AlpacaEval and MATH with candidates from a fixed policy.
CONTROLS: A scalar Bradley-Terry head on the same backbone and data, a generative judge of the same backbone prompted for pairwise verdicts, the distribution head with the entropy term removed, and reliability diagrams of expected level against human absolute ratings held out from HelpSteer2, over three seeds.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: We expect ranking accuracy within a point of the scalar head and better separation of good from bad responses at a fixed threshold on held-out absolute ratings. Calibration may fail on domains absent from the pairwise data, such as code.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Beta-distributed rewards that carry annotator disagreement
PROPOSAL: We train a reward head that outputs the two shape parameters of a Beta distribution over the quality of a response on the unit interval. For a pair, the training target is the probability that a draw for the chosen response exceeds a draw for the rejected one, computed in closed form, so that pairs on which annotators would disagree are fitted by overlapping distributions rather than by a large score gap. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-instruct on HelpSteer2-Preference, which records several annotators per pair, and on UltraFeedback, and we test whether the predicted variance tracks the observed annotator split, whether the mean serves as an absolute score, and whether Best-of-N selection on AlpacaEval and GSM8K improves when candidates with high variance are discounted.
CONTROLS: A scalar Bradley-Terry head on the same backbone and data, the Beta head trained on majority labels with the split discarded, a head trained on labels shuffled within prompt as placebo, correlation of predicted variance with annotator split on held-out pairs, three seeds.
COST: 640
PREDICTION: We expect predicted variance to correlate clearly with annotator split and ranking accuracy to match the scalar head. Discounting high-variance candidates should help Best-of-N on chat and not on arithmetic, where disagreement is rare.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ordinal thresholds anchor pairwise rewards to an absolute scale
PROPOSAL: We model response quality as a latent scalar from a reward head and learn a set of ordered cut points that map the latent to five quality bins, as in cumulative-link ordinal regression. Pairwise preference pairs train the latent through a Bradley-Terry likelihood, and a small set of pointwise ratings from HelpSteer2 trains the cut points and a single affine map of the latent, so that the abundant pairwise data fixes the ranking and the scarce absolute data fixes the scale. We fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-instruct on Skywork-Reward-Preference for the pairwise part, vary the number of pointwise ratings from a few dozen to the full set, and evaluate ranking accuracy on RewardBench, bin accuracy against held-out ratings, and the precision of a fixed acceptance threshold on chat, mathematics and code candidates.
CONTROLS: A scalar Bradley-Terry head with scores standardised per domain, the same head followed by Platt scaling on the pointwise ratings, a head trained on pointwise ratings alone, and cut points fitted to shuffled ratings as placebo, each over three seeds.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: We expect the ranking accuracy to stay unchanged while bin accuracy rises steeply with the first hundred ratings and then saturates. Threshold precision should transfer across domains better than for standardised scalar scores, which fail where the domain mean shifts.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Predicting the annotator split instead of the majority label
PROPOSAL: We train a reward model to predict, for a pair of responses, the fraction of annotators who prefer the first one, using the per-pair agreement counts available in HelpSteer2-Preference and in the multi-annotator subset of PKU-SafeRLHF, with a cross-entropy loss against the soft label rather than the majority vote. The model keeps a pointwise head, so the pairwise probability is a sigmoid of the score difference, and the scale of the scores is then fixed by the soft labels themselves, because a pair split evenly must receive equal scores. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-instruct, evaluate calibration of the predicted split against held-out agreement on the same datasets, ranking accuracy on RewardBench and RM-Bench, and the behaviour of a fixed threshold on absolute ratings from HelpSteer2.
CONTROLS: The same model trained on majority labels, a model trained on single-annotator subsamples to mimic ordinary preference data, a model trained on soft labels shuffled across pairs as placebo, expected calibration error on held-out splits, and three seeds.
COST: 560
PREDICTION: We expect soft-label training to give lower calibration error and equal ranking accuracy, and the predicted split to flag the pairs on which held-out annotators disagree. The scale fixed by soft labels may still drift across domains, which the threshold evaluation will reveal.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A verbal confidence token after a short critique as a calibrated reward
PROPOSAL: We fine-tune a generative reward model that, given a single response, writes a critique of at most three sentences and then emits one of ten confidence tokens standing for the probability that the response meets the task's requirements. Training uses pairwise data from UltraFeedback and Skywork-Reward-Preference through a Bradley-Terry likelihood on the expected confidence, with the critique supervised by distillation from a larger judge on a small subset, and a few hundred pointwise ratings from HelpSteer2 recalibrating the token-to-probability map. We use Llama-3.1-8B-instruct as backbone, cap the critique length so that scoring stays close to the latency of a discriminative pass, and evaluate ranking accuracy on RewardBench, Best-of-N gains on AlpacaEval and MATH, and calibration against held-out ratings.
CONTROLS: A scalar Bradley-Terry head on the same backbone and data, the same generative model without critique, a pairwise generative judge of the same backbone, a token-to-probability map fitted on shuffled ratings as placebo, and a measurement of scoring latency per response for each variant.
COST: 720
PREDICTION: We expect the critique to add a few points of ranking accuracy on reasoning and little elsewhere, and calibration to match that of the pointwise-anchored head. Latency will exceed that of the scalar head by the critique length, which may make the gain not worth it at large N.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Grounding a pairwise-trained reward model in code generation with few absolute labels
PROPOSAL: We adapt a reward model that learned only from chat preferences to code generation, where absolute labels are expensive to obtain, by collecting a few hundred pointwise correctness ratings on candidate solutions to problems from a held-out slice of a programming benchmark with unit tests, and we compare three ways of using them: fitting an affine recalibration of the score, fitting ordinal cut points, and fine-tuning the whole head with a pointwise loss on top of the pairwise one. We start from a Llama-3.1-8B-instruct reward model that we trained on Skywork-Reward-Preference, we vary the number of ratings, and we measure how well a fixed threshold predicts unit-test success and how ranking accuracy on code pairs from RewardBench changes.
CONTROLS: The unadapted model with a threshold tuned on chat, the unadapted model with scores standardised on code, ratings shuffled across candidates as placebo, a model trained on code pairs alone, and three seeds.
COST: 320
PREDICTION: We expect affine recalibration to recover most of the threshold precision with a few dozen ratings and the ordinal variant to win once ratings reach a few hundred. Full fine-tuning may lose ranking accuracy on chat, which we will report.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Threshold transfer across domains for scalar and probabilistic reward heads
PROPOSAL: We test whether a single acceptance threshold keeps its meaning across domains. For a scalar Bradley-Terry head and for a probabilistic head that outputs a distribution over quality levels, both fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-7B-instruct on the same pairwise data, we tune a threshold on absolute ratings from one domain and apply it unchanged to chat, mathematics, code and role-play candidates with held-out absolute ratings, measuring precision and recall of the accept decision in each domain and the drift of the score distribution of rated-good responses across domains.
CONTROLS: A threshold re-tuned per domain as the ceiling, a random threshold as the floor, the scalar head with per-domain standardisation, the probabilistic head with its pointwise anchoring removed, and a prevalence shift test where the fraction of good candidates is varied to check that the decision does not depend on it, over three seeds.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: We expect the scalar head's threshold to lose most of its precision when the domain changes, with the score of rated-good responses shifting by more than the gap between good and bad within a domain, and the probabilistic head to keep precision within a few points. Role-play, whose quality is most disputed among annotators, may defeat both.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Pointwise probabilistic scoring against a generative judge at matched inference
PROPOSAL: Compare, at equal scoring work per candidate, a pointwise reward head that outputs a probability of acceptability with a generative judge that writes a critique before its verdict, both built on Llama-3.1-8B-instruct and trained from the same pairwise data from UltraFeedback. Score candidate sets from a fixed policy on AlpacaEval, MATH and a code benchmark with N from two to sixty-four, select the best candidate under each scorer, and record the quality of the selection as judged by held-out human ratings and unit tests, together with the scoring latency and the accuracy of each scorer's own confidence about its verdict.
CONTROLS: A scalar Bradley-Terry head, the generative judge with its critique removed, the generative judge with a critique length cap matching the pointwise head's latency, random selection as the floor, an oracle selection as the ceiling, and three seeds for training and for sampling candidates.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: We expect the pointwise head to match the judge at small N and to pull ahead as N grows because the judge's pairwise format needs many comparisons. The judge should win on mathematics, where a critique catches wrong steps, and its advantage should vanish once its critique is capped.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evidential reward heads that flag inconsistent preference pairs
PROPOSAL: We train a reward head that outputs the parameters of a Dirichlet distribution over five quality levels, so that the model expresses both a quality estimate and how much evidence supports it, and we train it from pairwise data through the probability, under the Dirichlet, that the chosen response's expected level exceeds the rejected one's. We then use the evidence term to flag training pairs the model finds inconsistent, retrain after removing the flagged pairs, and measure whether ranking accuracy on RewardBench and RM-Bench improves and whether the evidence term predicts annotator disagreement on HelpSteer2-Preference. Backbones are Llama-3.1-8B-instruct and Gemma-2-9B-it, trained on Skywork-Reward-Preference.
CONTROLS: A scalar Bradley-Terry head with and without the same fraction of pairs removed at random, removal based on the scalar head's loss instead of evidence, a Dirichlet head without the evidence regulariser, correlation of evidence with annotator split on held-out pairs, three seeds.
COST: 960
PREDICTION: We expect the evidence term to predict annotator split better than the scalar head's loss and the filtered retraining to gain a point or two of ranking accuracy on the chat subsets. Removing the same fraction at random should gain nothing, otherwise the gain is from data volume.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Per-pair temperature from annotator disagreement in the pairwise loss
PROPOSAL: We modify the Bradley-Terry loss so that each pair has its own temperature, set from the recorded annotator agreement on that pair when available and otherwise predicted by a small auxiliary head trained on the pairs where it is available, so that contested pairs push the scores less than unanimous ones. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-instruct on HelpSteer2-Preference, which has per-pair agreement counts, and on Skywork-Reward-Preference, which has none, and we evaluate ranking accuracy on RewardBench and RM-Bench, calibration of the sigmoid of score differences against held-out agreement, and whether a fixed threshold on scores separates responses by held-out absolute rating.
CONTROLS: Standard Bradley-Terry with a single temperature, the per-pair temperature set from a shuffled assignment of agreement counts as placebo, the auxiliary head alone as a predictor of disagreement, and three seeds.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: We expect a small gain in ranking accuracy and a clear gain in calibration on the dataset with agreement counts, and a smaller transfer of both through the auxiliary head to the dataset without. The threshold test should show little change, because the temperature reshapes score differences and not the scale.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A categorical quality head on pairwise data, tested against the scalar head it replaces
PROPOSAL: We replace the scalar value head of a discriminative reward model with a categorical head over five quality levels, train it on Skywork-Reward-Preference through a Bradley-Terry likelihood on the expected level, and anchor the level scale with a small set of pointwise ratings from HelpSteer2. Backbones are Llama-3.1-8B-instruct and Gemma-2-9B-it. We report ranking accuracy on RewardBench, Best-of-N gains on AlpacaEval and MATH, and calibration of the expected level against held-out ratings.
CONTROLS: A scalar Bradley-Terry head on the same backbone, data and schedule; a generative pairwise judge of the same backbone; the categorical head with no pointwise anchoring and with the full pointwise set, to bound what anchoring adds; reliability diagrams and expected calibration error against held-out ratings; a fixed-threshold precision test on chat, mathematics and code candidates; three seeds with confidence intervals from bootstrap over prompts.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: We expect ranking accuracy within a point of the scalar head, clearly better calibration, and higher fixed-threshold precision on domains present in the anchoring set. Calibration on code, absent from the anchoring set, may fail.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Replacing the scalar reward head with a categorical quality distribution
PROPOSAL: A categorical head over five quality levels replaces the scalar value head of a discriminative reward model and is trained on Skywork-Reward-Preference through a Bradley-Terry likelihood on the expected level, with a small set of pointwise ratings from HelpSteer2 fixing the level scale. We use Llama-3.1-8B-instruct and Gemma-2-9B-it as backbones and report ranking accuracy on RewardBench, Best-of-N gains on AlpacaEval and MATH, and the agreement of the expected level with held-out ratings.
CONTROLS: Learning-rate schedules with cosine and with linear decay; a sweep of the number of quality levels from three to nine; training with two different tokenisation settings for the chat template; the training and validation loss curves of the categorical head, reported per epoch; a check that the expected level is monotone in the categorical logits; and a comparison of RewardBench accuracy with the public leaderboard entries of reward models of similar size trained on other data.
COST: 480
PREDICTION: We expect accuracy near the leaderboard entries of similar size and the agreement with ratings to rise with the number of levels up to about seven. Cosine decay should train more stably than linear.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Soft preference targets to capture annotator disagreement in a reward model
PROPOSAL: We train a pointwise reward model to predict the fraction of annotators who prefer one response over another, using the per-pair counts of HelpSteer2-Preference and of the multi-annotator subset of PKU-SafeRLHF, with a cross-entropy loss against the soft label. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-instruct and ask whether the predicted split matches held-out annotator behaviour and whether ranking accuracy on RewardBench is preserved.
CONTROLS: The same model trained on the majority label, which is the standard practice the question asks us to improve on; a model trained on soft labels shuffled across pairs, as placebo; training on a single annotator drawn per pair, to mimic ordinary preference data; expected calibration error and a reliability diagram of predicted split against held-out agreement; the correlation of predicted split with held-out annotator split; and three seeds with bootstrap intervals over pairs.
COST: 640
PREDICTION: We expect calibration error to halve relative to majority-label training with no loss of ranking accuracy, and the predicted split to identify most pairs on which held-out annotators disagree. If the shuffled placebo calibrates equally well, the model only learned the base rate of disagreement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward models trained on annotator vote fractions rather than majority labels
PROPOSAL: A pointwise reward model learns to predict, for each pair of responses, the fraction of annotators who preferred the first, from the per-pair vote counts of HelpSteer2-Preference and the multi-annotator subset of PKU-SafeRLHF, with a cross-entropy loss against the soft label in place of the usual hard label. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B-instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-instruct, report ranking accuracy on RewardBench and RM-Bench, and plot the predicted fractions against held-out vote fractions.
CONTROLS: A sweep of dropout over four values; maximum sequence lengths of two thousand and four thousand tokens; two orderings of the training data, random and sorted by prompt length; accelerator memory per configuration; the fluency of responses sampled from a policy trained against each reward model, judged by a larger model; and the loss curves of the soft-label model, inspected for divergence.
COST: 640
PREDICTION: We expect stable training under both orderings and the predicted fractions to track held-out votes on most pairs. Policies trained against the soft-label model should read as fluently as those trained against the standard one.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Whether a fixed acceptance threshold keeps its meaning across domains
PROPOSAL: We tune an acceptance threshold for a reward model on absolute ratings from chat and apply it unchanged to mathematics, code, safety and role-play candidates with held-out absolute ratings, comparing a scalar Bradley-Terry head with a probabilistic head over quality levels anchored by a few hundred pointwise ratings, both fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-7B-instruct on the same pairwise data. We measure precision and recall of the accept decision per domain.
CONTROLS: A threshold re-tuned per domain, as the ceiling the transferred threshold is measured against; a random threshold as the floor; the scalar head with per-domain standardisation of scores, the strongest cheap fix; the probabilistic head with its anchoring removed; a prevalence shift in which the fraction of good candidates is varied from a tenth to nine tenths, to check that precision does not depend on it; and three seeds.
COST: 320
PREDICTION: We expect the scalar head's transferred threshold to lose most of its precision outside chat and the anchored probabilistic head to keep it within a few points, with standardisation recovering part of the loss. Role-play may defeat both because its ratings disagree most.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Acceptance thresholds on reward scores across chat, mathematics and code
PROPOSAL: For a scalar Bradley-Terry head and a probabilistic head over quality levels, both fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-7B-instruct on the same pairwise data and the latter anchored by a few hundred pointwise ratings, we tune an acceptance threshold on absolute ratings from chat and apply it to mathematics, code, safety and role-play candidates with held-out absolute ratings, measuring precision and recall of the accept decision per domain.
CONTROLS: A table of precision and recall at five thresholds per head, reported for each domain; receiver operating characteristic curves on the chat domain, where the threshold was tuned; pairwise ranking accuracy of each head on RewardBench, as a check of general quality; a regression of each head's score on response length within each domain; and a comparison of the chat-domain precision with the accuracies published for the two heads' training data.
COST: 320
PREDICTION: We expect both heads to show high precision on chat and the probabilistic head to keep more of it on the other domains. Scores should correlate with length on chat more than on code.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: How many absolute ratings anchor a pairwise-trained reward model to a scale
PROPOSAL: We train a reward head on Skywork-Reward-Preference with a Bradley-Terry likelihood and add ordinal cut points fitted on pointwise ratings from HelpSteer2, varying the number of ratings from zero through tens and hundreds to the full set, on Llama-3.1-8B-instruct. We measure bin accuracy against held-out ratings, fixed-threshold precision across domains, and ranking accuracy on RewardBench after each setting.
CONTROLS: Zero ratings, which shows what pairwise data alone gives; the same pairwise head followed by Platt scaling on the identical ratings, the simplest use of them; a head trained on the ratings alone with no pairwise data, to show what the pairwise data adds; cut points fitted on shuffled ratings, as placebo; ranking accuracy measured before and after anchoring, to confirm that the scale does not come at the price of ranking; and three seeds with bootstrap intervals over the rating subsets.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: We expect bin accuracy to rise steeply with the first hundred ratings and then flatten, and ranking accuracy to stay unchanged. If Platt scaling matches ordinal cut points at every size, the cut points add nothing beyond an affine map.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Anchoring a pairwise reward model with a handful of absolute ratings
PROPOSAL: A reward head learns from Skywork-Reward-Preference with a Bradley-Terry likelihood, and ordinal cut points fitted on pointwise ratings from HelpSteer2 map its scores to quality bins. We vary the number of ratings from tens through hundreds to the full set, on Llama-3.1-8B-instruct, and we measure bin accuracy against held-out ratings and fixed-threshold precision on chat, mathematics and code candidates, reporting the rating count at which each measure stops improving.
CONTROLS: The wording of the rating instructions given to annotators, in two variants; the optimiser, with and without weight decay; the number of epochs over the ratings, from one to five; a report of the per-epoch training loss on the cut points; the accuracy on MT-Bench of a policy trained against the anchored model, judged by a larger model; and the time taken to fit the cut points at each rating count.
COST: 400
PREDICTION: We expect bin accuracy to rise with rating count and to depend little on the optimiser. The policy's MT-Bench accuracy should be unchanged by anchoring, since the ranking is unchanged.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Pointwise probabilistic scoring versus a critique-writing judge at matched inference
PROPOSAL: We compare, for Best-of-N selection, a pointwise head that outputs a probability of acceptability with a generative judge that writes a critique and then a verdict, both on Llama-3.1-8B-instruct and trained from UltraFeedback pairs. Candidates come from a fixed policy on AlpacaEval, MATH and a code benchmark, with N swept from two to sixty-four, and selections are judged by held-out human ratings and unit tests.
CONTROLS: Equal backbone size and equal training pairs for both scorers; the generative judge with its critique capped to match the pointwise head's token count, so that the comparison is at equal inference; a scalar Bradley-Terry head; the judge without any critique; random selection as the floor and oracle selection as the ceiling; ranking accuracy on RewardBench alongside Best-of-N gains, since they can diverge; and bootstrap intervals over prompts with three training seeds.
COST: 560
PREDICTION: We expect the pointwise head to match the judge at small N and to win at large N, and the judge to win on mathematics until its critique is capped. If the capped judge still wins, the critique's gain does not come from its length.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A critique-writing judge against a pointwise probabilistic head for Best-of-N
PROPOSAL: A generative judge that writes a critique before its verdict and a pointwise head that outputs a probability of acceptability, both built on Llama-3.1-8B-instruct from UltraFeedback pairs, select the best candidate from sets sampled by a fixed policy on AlpacaEval, MATH and a code benchmark, with N swept from two to sixty-four, and we record the quality of each selection under held-out human ratings and unit tests, together with the latency of each scorer.
CONTROLS: Decoding temperature of the judge at three settings; four wordings of the judge's instruction, to measure prompt sensitivity; batch sizes for scoring, to show throughput; key-value caching on and off for the judge; the judge's accuracy on a trivia question-answering set, as a check of its general ability; and the agreement between two judge runs with different sampling seeds.
COST: 560
PREDICTION: We expect the judge's selections to vary with prompt wording by a few points and its latency to exceed the pointwise head's by the critique length. The two scorers should agree on most candidate sets at small N.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Disagreement-aware probabilistic reward heads evaluated on calibration and ranking
PROPOSAL: We train a reward head that outputs a Beta distribution over quality on the unit interval, fitting pairs through the closed-form probability that a draw for the chosen response exceeds one for the rejected, so that contested pairs are fitted by overlapping distributions. We fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-instruct on HelpSteer2-Preference and UltraFeedback and measure whether predicted variance tracks annotator split, whether the mean works as an absolute score under a fixed threshold, and whether ranking accuracy on RewardBench holds.
CONTROLS: A scalar Bradley-Terry head on the same data, the Beta head trained on majority labels only, labels shuffled within prompt as placebo, correlation of variance with held-out annotator split, and three seeds.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: We expect variance to correlate clearly with annotator split, ranking accuracy to match the scalar head, and threshold precision to improve on chat. If the majority-label Beta head shows the same variance pattern, the spread reflects prompt difficulty rather than disagreement.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Cleaning preference data by majority filtering before scalar reward training
PROPOSAL: We improve a scalar Bradley-Terry reward model by cleaning its training data: on HelpSteer2-Preference and UltraFeedback we keep only pairs whose annotators or rating gaps agree unanimously, drop every contested pair, and augment the remainder with pairs relabelled by a larger model when it agrees with the majority. We fine-tune Llama-3.1-8B-instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-instruct on the cleaned set and measure ranking accuracy on RewardBench and RM-Bench and Best-of-N gains on AlpacaEval.
CONTROLS: The same head trained on the uncleaned data, cleaning by random removal of the same number of pairs, cleaning by the larger model alone without agreement counts, Best-of-N gains at two values of N, and three seeds.
COST: 800
PREDICTION: We expect cleaned training to gain a point or two of ranking accuracy over the full data and more than random removal. Gains should be largest on the chat subsets, where contested pairs are most frequent.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Ordinal cut points to ground a pairwise reward model in an absolute scale
PROPOSAL: We fit a reward head on Skywork-Reward-Preference through a Bradley-Terry likelihood and learn ordered cut points mapping its score to quality bins from a small set of pointwise ratings in HelpSteer2, so that abundant pairs fix the ranking and scarce ratings fix the scale. On Llama-3.1-70B-instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-instruct we vary the number of ratings and measure bin accuracy on held-out ratings, fixed-threshold precision across chat, mathematics and code, and ranking accuracy on RewardBench.
CONTROLS: A scalar head with per-domain standardisation, the same head with Platt scaling on the ratings, a head trained on ratings alone, cut points fitted to shuffled ratings, and three seeds.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect bin accuracy to saturate after the first few hundred ratings and ranking accuracy to be untouched, with the larger backbone needing fewer ratings. If Platt scaling matches the cut points everywhere, an affine map suffices to ground the scale.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reinforcement-trained critiques to raise the pairwise accuracy of a generative judge
PROPOSAL: We train a generative judge on Llama-3.1-70B-instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-instruct to write a critique of two responses and then name the better one, using reinforcement learning with a reward of one when the named response matches the preferred one in Skywork-Reward-Preference, with a length penalty on the critique and eight sampled critiques per pair during training. We measure pairwise accuracy on RewardBench and RM-Bench and the length of the critiques, and we test whether sampling several critiques at inference and voting raises accuracy further.
CONTROLS: The same judge trained by supervised fine-tuning on critiques from a larger model, the judge without any critique, a scalar Bradley-Terry head of the same backbone, voting over one, four and sixteen critiques, and three seeds.
COST: 1200
PREDICTION: We expect the reinforcement-trained judge to exceed the scalar head on reasoning pairs and to trail it on chat, with voting adding a few points at a rising inference price. Critiques should get longer during training unless the length penalty is strong.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Fixed-threshold acceptance with calibrated probabilities across five domains
PROPOSAL: We give a reward model a head that outputs the probability that a response meets the task's requirements, train it on UltraFeedback pairs with a Bradley-Terry likelihood on the log-odds and anchor it with a few hundred pointwise ratings from HelpSteer2, on Qwen2.5-7B-instruct. We then fix the acceptance threshold at one half and measure precision and recall of the accept decision on chat, mathematics, code, safety and role-play candidates with held-out ratings, to learn whether one threshold works everywhere.
CONTROLS: A scalar head with a threshold tuned on chat, a scalar head with per-domain standardisation, the probabilistic head without anchoring, a threshold re-tuned per domain as ceiling, a prevalence shift test, and three seeds.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: We expect the fixed threshold to keep precision within a few points across chat, mathematics and code and to fail on role-play, where ratings disagree most. If the unanchored head does as well, the pairwise data alone already fixes the scale.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: What a reward model rewards, regressing scores on surface features of responses
PROPOSAL: We take a scalar Bradley-Terry reward model fine-tuned from Qwen2.5-7B-instruct on UltraFeedback pairs and explain its scores by regressing them, on chat, mathematics, code, safety and role-play candidates, on surface features of the response: length in tokens, number of list items, number of headings, presence of code blocks, reading-level score, count of hedging phrases and sentiment. We report the variance explained per domain, the sign of each feature's coefficient, and the change in score when each feature is edited in a controlled rewrite of the same response by a larger model.
CONTROLS: The same regression on a reward model trained on a second preference set, the regression on held-out candidates, feature values shuffled across responses as placebo, and three seeds for the reward model.
COST: 240
PREDICTION: We expect length and list count to explain a large share of score variance on chat and little on mathematics. Controlled rewrites should move the score in the direction of the coefficients on most domains.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Variance-aware Best-of-N selection from a probabilistic reward head
PROPOSAL: We train a reward head on Llama-3.1-8B-instruct that outputs a mean and a variance of quality per response, fitted on Skywork-Reward-Preference pairs through the probability that a Gaussian draw for the chosen response exceeds one for the rejected, with the variance regularised toward the annotator split recorded in HelpSteer2-Preference. At selection time we rank candidates by a lower quantile of their distribution rather than by the mean, on AlpacaEval, MATH and a code benchmark with N up to sixty-four, and judge selections by held-out ratings and unit tests.
CONTROLS: Selection by the mean of the same head, a scalar Bradley-Terry head, a head with the variance regulariser removed, three quantile levels, random and oracle selection, and three seeds.
COST: 960
PREDICTION: We expect quantile selection to beat mean selection at large N on chat, where high-mean high-variance candidates are often rated poorly, and to make no difference on mathematics. If the unregularised head's variance works as well, the annotator split adds nothing.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scaling preference data with synthetic pairs labelled by a larger model
PROPOSAL: We expand the training set of a scalar Bradley-Terry reward model on Llama-3.1-8B-instruct by generating candidate responses from several policies for prompts drawn from a general instruction corpus, labelling each pair with a larger model's verdict, and adding the synthetic pairs to Skywork-Reward-Preference in ratios from equal size to eight times the original. We measure ranking accuracy on RewardBench and RM-Bench and Best-of-N gains on AlpacaEval, MATH and a code benchmark with N up to sixty-four, judged by held-out ratings and unit tests.
CONTROLS: The head trained on the original pairs alone, synthetic pairs with labels from a smaller model, synthetic pairs with labels flipped at random for a fifth of them, the original data duplicated to the same size, and three seeds.
COST: 960
PREDICTION: We expect ranking accuracy to rise with synthetic data up to about four times the original and then flatten, with the gain concentrated on domains the original data covers poorly. Duplicated data should give no gain.

PROPOSAL: We adapt a reward model trained on chat preferences to a safety domain where absolute ratings are scarce: starting from a Llama-3.1-8B-instruct head trained on Skywork-Reward-Preference, we select candidate responses from PKU-SafeRLHF prompts for pointwise rating either at random or by the head's own uncertainty, obtain a few hundred ratings, and fit ordinal cut points on them while keeping the pairwise loss active.
